rendered:
The review says tumor metastasis [1] main steps, shown in Fig. 1[2]:

- Local invasion at the primary tumor site. Through epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), tumor cells take on stem-cell traits and become invasive, which lets them break away from the primary site.[3][4][5]
- Intravasation into the circulatory system. Vessels formed by cancer cells are often incomplete, tortuous and leaky, which makes it easier for tumor cells to pass into and out of the bloodstream.[6][7][8]
- Survival in circulation. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) bind to platelets and form tumor emboli. This shields them from shear forces, gives them access to growth factors such as TGF-β that support EMT, and protects them from natural killer (NK) cells.[9][10][11][12]
- Extravasation into distant organs. CTCs pass through the vessel walls of distant organs into the tissue, which sets up colonization. Most of the cells that get through become dormant and avoid immune clearance.[13][14][15][16]
- Colonization and growth. Cells adapt to the new microenvironment. Dormant cells reactivate only after that microenvironment is remodeled, often through inflammatory signals or myeloid-derived suppressor cells. They then multiply and form lethal macro-metastases.[17][18][19]

One inconsistency: the caption of the figure also says "five key steps" but lists only intravasation, survival in circulation, extravasation, and colonization and growth. It leaves out local invasion, which the main text includes.[20]
